habitat: Eastern long-necked turtles are found in eastern Australia, from Queensland through New South Wales and Victoria to South Australia. They inhabit slow-moving rivers, swamps, billabongs, lakes, and farm dams — almost any permanent or semi-permanent freshwater body. During dry periods, they may travel overland to find water. They spend much of their time basking on logs and banks but are strong swimmers and can remain submerged for hours. They are among Australia's most common and recognizable freshwater turtles.
diet: Eastern long-necked turtles are carnivorous ambush predators, feeding on aquatic insects, tadpoles, small fish, crustaceans, mollusks, and carrion. They employ a unique hunting strategy: rather than actively chasing prey, they lie in wait and rapidly extend their extraordinarily long, flexible neck to strike — similar to a snake's strike. This serpentine neck, which bends sideways rather than retracting straight back, can reach prey at surprising distances. In captivity, they adapt to commercial turtle pellets and chopped seafood.
behavior: Eastern long-necked turtles are primarily nocturnal foragers, spending daylight hours basking or resting on the bottom. When threatened, rather than withdrawing into their shell (which they cannot fully do due to their long neck), they emit a foul-smelling musk from glands near their legs — a pungent defense that gives them the nickname 'stinker.' Females dig nests in soft soil up to 150 meters from water, laying 8-24 eggs which incubate for 3-5 months. They are surprisingly mobile on land, often crossing roads in search of nesting sites or new water bodies.
facts: The eastern long-necked turtle has a neck that can be as long as or longer than its shell. Instead of retracting directly into the shell like most turtles, it bends the neck sideways (pleurodirous) — a trait shared with all side-necked turtles. Their shell, or carapace, is broad, flat, and dark brown to black, reaching 25-30 cm. They are exceptionally long-lived, with lifespans of 30-50 years in the wild. They are common in the Australian pet trade and are known for their curious, interactive personalities.
naming: Eastern long-necked turtle names might reflect their serpentine neck, Australian origin, or musky defense. Consider names like Serpent, Stretch, Longo, Snakey, Billabong, Ozzie, Dundee, Koopa, Snappy, Sidewinder, Neo (long-neck), or Digger.
